clue.text: Without hesitation the composer makes his mark

indicators.note: without tells us to leave the hesitation sound out of the composer's name

parts.note: Sir John Stainer was a Victorian English composer of church music
er is the sound a speaker makes when hesitating

explanation.surface: A composer finally signs his name decisively, with no dithering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' removes ER from STAINER, leaving the five letters; 'makes his' just joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To stain something is to leave a blot or blemish on it, which is to mark it.

clue.text: Californian city lacks nothing for a holy rite

indicators.note: lacks tells us the city name goes without the letter for nothing

parts.note: Sacramento is the state capital of California
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A city in California is fully supplied for a religious ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacks nothing' reads as 'has everything', but it says take O (nothing) from SACRAMENTO.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacrament is a Christian ceremony such as baptism or communion, a sacred observance.

clue.text: Hard for both man and insect

parts.note: Adam was the first man in Genesis
an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: Life is tough for people and bugs alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant originally named a legendary unbreakable stone, so as an adjective it means unyielding.

clue.text: Value of a horse-shoe fixer in Gloucestershire

parts.note: a nail fixes a shoe to a horse's hoof; the possessive reading gives NAILS
worth means value

explanation.surface: What a farrier's nail is worth, somewhere in the west of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'value of a horse-shoe fixer' as NAIL'S WORTH; Nailsworth is a small town in Gloucestershire, an English county in the Cotswolds.
explanation.definitionFit: Nailsworth is a market town near Stroud, so it is a place found in that county.

clue.text: Like a juicy peach, or a cactus for instance

explanation.surface: Describing a ripe fruit, or a desert plant, with the same adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Juicy fruit is full of sap and fleshy; a cactus is the standard example of a plant with thick water-storing tissue, a botanical noun for such plants.

clue.text: A winter sport rule maker may be parsimonious

parts.note: skiing is a winter sport; ski is the short form
an MP, Member of Parliament, makes laws

explanation.surface: A ski-loving lawmaker could turn out to be a penny-pincher.
explanation.walkthrough: An MP is a Member of Parliament, who votes on the laws, hence 'rule maker'.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp is to spend or supply too little, to be stingy.

clue.text: Is able to get many varied meals at the feast

parts.note: can means is able to
D is the Roman numeral for 500, a large number

indicators.note: varied means altered or rearranged, so the letters of meals are mixed

explanation.surface: Someone can have lots of different dishes at the banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'many' gives D (500); 'varied' turns MEALS into LEMAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Candlemas, on 2 February, is a church festival, a feast day in the Christian calendar.

clue.text: A cosh or plastic surgery for this customer?

definitions.text: A cosh or plastic surgery for this customer?

parts.words: A cosh or plastic surgery for this customer?
parts.note: a violent, threatening person may carry a cosh, while a plain-looking one might seek cosmetic surgery: both fit the phrase for a nasty or unattractive type

explanation.surface: Asks whether a club or a facelift suits a particular person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An ugly customer' is a dangerous person (who might use a cosh); 'ugly' also means plain-looking, needing plastic surgery. A cosh is a short club.
explanation.definitionFit: An ugly customer is a dangerous person; the adjective also means unsightly, the two senses the clue plays on.

clue.text: Plan measurement of East African pungency

parts.note: A is an abbreviation for African
a sting is a sharp, biting quality

explanation.surface: Measuring how fiery an East African dish is.
explanation.walkthrough: On a map grid an easting is the distance measured eastwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An easting is a grid coordinate on a map or survey plan, a distance in one direction.

clue.text: Piquant, thanks to the pen

parts.note: ta is informal British for thank you
a sty is a pen for pigs

explanation.surface: Thanks to the writer's pen, the prose has a sharp flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: Something piquant is pleasantly sharp, full of flavour.

clue.text: Fusion of fuel gets one into trouble

parts.note: coal is a fuel burned in fires and furnaces
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: trouble, used as a verb, means stir up or disturb, so the letters that follow are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Fuel lands someone in hot water, perhaps through a merger gone wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' looks like a link word but is part of the anagram: 'trouble' stirs I (one) and INTO into ITION, which follows COAL; 'gets' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A coalition is a union or merging of parties, a political synonym for fusion.

clue.text: Which one entered to challenge inventories

explanation.surface: Someone stepped forward to dispute the stock lists.
explanation.walkthrough: In medieval jousting the lists were the enclosed ground a knight entered to challenge an opponent.
explanation.definitionFit: The tilting arena of a tournament was called the lists; inventories are catalogues of items, written records of goods.

clue.text: A mother's present for teacher.? A bit throaty!

parts.note: a dam is the mother of an animal, here possessive
an apple is the traditional gift a pupil brings a teacher

explanation.surface: A mother gives a gift to the schoolteacher, who is touched and a bit choked.
explanation.walkthrough: A dam is an animal's mother (a horse breeder's term), so 'mother's' gives DAM'S.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adam's apple is the lump of cartilage at the front of the neck, a part of the throat.

clue.text: Short measure for' this tot

parts.note: a tot is both a small measure of spirits and a small child, so the clue describes the child by the size of the drink

explanation.surface: A barman pours a small measure for a child.
explanation.walkthrough: A tot of rum is a short measure; a tot is also a toddler, and both are very small.
explanation.definitionFit: A tot is a little child, and the adjective here describes that smallness: very small, minute.

clue.text: The function of one of the neighbouring columns

definitions.text: The function of one of the neighbouring columns

parts.words: The function of one of the neighbouring columns
parts.note: in the paper the crossword sat beside the personal columns of births, marriages and deaths, whose job is making things public

explanation.surface: Asks what one of the nearby pillars is for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'columns' suggests pillars, but means newspaper columns next to the puzzle, such as the announcements of births and deaths.
explanation.definitionFit: Those columns exist to make public declarations, which is the job named.

clue.text: Work in an alley-a feature of thermodynamics

indicators.note: in places the work inside the alley

parts.note: an entry is a regional word for a narrow passage between houses
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: Work done in a back lane somehow links up with heat physics.
explanation.walkthrough: ENTRY is a northern English word for an alley between terraced houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Entropy is the measure of disorder in a system, a central quantity in the second law of heat physics.

clue.text: Where three quarters only take riding

definitions.text: Where three quarters only take riding

parts.words: Where three quarters only take riding
parts.note: the county was historically divided into three Ridings, from Old Norse for thirds, rather than four parts

explanation.surface: A place where most of the population goes horse riding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'riding' looks like horseback, but the Ridings were the three historic divisions of this English county: North, East and West.
explanation.definitionFit: The big northern county was split into three Ridings, so its 'quarters' were thirds.

clue.text: A stable article about a runner

indicators.note: about means going round, so the stable article encloses the A

parts.note: a manger is the feeding trough found in a stable

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece on a racehorse from a stable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests a racehorse, which fits the stable, but here it is someone who runs a business.
explanation.definitionFit: A manager runs a firm or team, so a runner in the sense of the person in charge.

clue.text: Members holding highest places in the House

definitions.text: Members holding highest places in the House

parts.words: Members holding highest places in the House
parts.note: 'Members' and 'House' suggest Parliament, but these are timbers at the top of a building's roof

explanation.surface: MPs with the most senior seats in the Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' and 'House' point to Parliament; the members are beams at the ridge of a house.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooftree is a ridgepole, the beam along the peak of a roof, the top timber.

clue.text: A characteristic alternative to a good countryman

annotationWithheld.why: A characteristic alternative to a good countryman (7): TRAIT + OR needs 'alternative' for OR, but the definition 'alternative to a good countryman' also needs that word, so it does two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: A characteristic alternative to a good countryman

clue.text: Song about a bounder in rural paradise

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the song is placed round the bounder

parts.note: an aria is a song in an opera
a cad is a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: A ballad tells of a rogue in an idyllic countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: CAD and bounder are both old British words for an ungentlemanly man.
explanation.definitionFit: Arcadia, a region of Greece, became the poetic name for an idyllic pastoral land.

clue.text: Stingy type — that's one of the signs

explanation.surface: A mean person is described as belonging to some category.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stingy' is read as 'having a sting': the scorpion, symbol of this zodiac sign.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scorpion is a creature with a sting in its tail, and it is also the eighth sign of the zodiac.

clue.text: Succeed in getting parson into Jack's vessel

indicators.note: into puts the parson inside the vessel

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water
Rev is short for Reverend, a parson's title

explanation.surface: A vicar succeeds in getting aboard a sailor's ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' suggests a sailor and his ship, but it is the Jack of the rhyme with his pail.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevail is to triumph or win through.

clue.text: With all due deference' to speed

explanation.surface: Respectfully deferring to someone who is going fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin 'pace' prefaces a polite disagreement, meaning with respect to someone; it is also a rate of movement, like velocity.

clue.text: It comes from the press of a finger

definitions.text: It comes from the press of a finger

parts.words: It comes from the press of a finger
parts.note: 'press' suggests a ... press, but it is the pressing of a fingertip, which leaves a mark

explanation.surface: Something produced when a finger is pushed down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'press' looks like the printing press, which also produces this, but here it is a fingertip pressed onto a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A fingertip pressed on glass leaves an impression of its ridges, the kind police lift.

clue.text: Contracting can be a strain to a little man

indicators.note: can be signals that the letters of strain may be rearranged into another form

parts.note: the six letters of strain are the anagram fodder
gent is a shortened form of gentleman

explanation.surface: Making a deal can put pressure on a small person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' rearranges STRAIN into ASTRIN; GENT, short for gentleman, is the 'little man'.
explanation.definitionFit: An astringent substance makes body tissue draw together, so it is contracting or constricting.

clue.text: Best man in the country gets corrupted

indicators.note: in places the saint inside the country's abbreviation

parts.note: RUS is the international abbreviation for Russia
St, a saint, is the best of men

explanation.surface: The groom's best man in rural parts goes bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best man' suggests a wedding but means a saint, ST; 'the country' suggests the countryside but is RUS, Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron rusts when it oxidises and decays, so it is eaten away.

clue.text: Ruin often seen with these driving clouds

explanation.surface: Destruction comes alongside storm clouds blowing in.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'rack and ruin' pairs the two; 'these' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: Rack is destruction in the stock phrase rack and ruin; it also names broken clouds blown along by the wind.

clue.text: The end of Forster's' passage

parts.note: E. M. Forster's novel is A Passage to ..., so the passage's destination is the country of the title

explanation.surface: The last part of a piece of writing by Forster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passage' looks like a stretch of prose, but it is the voyage in the title of E. M. Forster's novel A Passage to India.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's title names the subcontinent nation as the passage's destination.

clue.text: After this, month there's one football crowd to encourage

indicators.note: after says the following pieces come behind the month abbreviation

parts.note: inst., short for instant, means of this month in old business letters
one is the Roman numeral I
the gate is the attendance at a football match

explanation.surface: Next month a crowd at the match will be urged on.
explanation.walkthrough: INST (instant) is the old commercial abbreviation for this month; the gate is the number paying to watch a match.
explanation.definitionFit: To instigate is to urge or provoke someone into action.

clue.text: "Cool shall fan the glade "(Pope)

parts.note: a line from Alexander Pope's pastoral Summer with one word left out; the missing word is the entry

explanation.surface: A line of pastoral verse by Alexander Pope with a word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash in the gap; the line in Pope's Summer is 'Cool gales shall fan the glade'.
explanation.definitionFit: The breezes of Pope's line are strong winds that cool the summer glade.
